about: The second of the three prayers, and from first word to last the priest's own: deliver me, my iniquities, make me cling. Fili Dei vivi is a quotation twice over — Peter says Tu es Christus, Filius Dei vivi at Caesarea Philippi, and Martha says it at Bethany before the raising of Lazarus; both Gospels stand in this missal. The relative clause names all three Persons at work in one redemption: by the will of the Father, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, through Thy own death. In Masses for the dead the first prayer is dropped, but this one is said.

s01.translation: O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God,

s02.translation: who by the will of the Father, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, hast by Thy death given life to the world:

s03.translation: deliver me by this Thy most holy Body and Blood from all my iniquities and from every evil:

s04.translation: and make me always cling to Thy commandments, and never allow me to be parted from Thee:

s05.translation: Who with the same God the Father and the Holy Spirit livest and reignest, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

w004.function: Vocative: fili, not filius. The title is Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi and Martha's at Bethany, both quoted here word for word.

w006.function: Agrees with “Dei” (w005), not with Fili: the God who is living, over against the gods that are not.

w011.function: Ablative absolute with “Spíritu” (w012): the Spirit working along with. A deponent participle — passive in form, active in meaning.

w016.function: Agrees with “mortem” (w015). Three Persons and three prepositional phrases stand side by side: from the Father, with the Spirit, through His own death.

w017.function: Object of “vivificásti” (w018): what was given life — not the Church, not the elect, but the world.

w018.function: A shortened perfect: vivificávisti with the -vi- squeezed out, as Latin regularly does. Whitaker's does not carry the contracted form, so this parse rests on Collatinus and the edition.

w020.function: The prayer turns to the first person singular here and stays there; the priest asks for himself alone.

w022.function: Neuter, agreeing with “Corpus” (w024): this Body — the one lying on the corporal in front of him.

w023.function: A Roman legal term: a sacrosánctus person could not be harmed without incurring a curse.

w027.function: Agrees with “Sánguinem” (w026) alone, being masculine, though the sense covers the neuter Corpus as well.

w030.function: Iniquity is what is not æquum, not level: the word draws its picture from a crooked line rather than from a broken law.

w034.function: Neuter plural, as in the embolism: evils, not evil men. The petition widens from his own sins to everything that harms.

w037.function: Subject of the infinitive “inhærére” (w040) in the accusative: make me to cling — one construction, two accusatives.

w038.function: Agrees with “mandátis” (w041), three words later; Latin can hold an adjective that far from its noun without ambiguity because the endings match.

w040.function: In and hæreo, to stick fast to — the same verb used of things glued together. It takes the dative.

w041.function: Dative after “inhærére” (w040): cling to what — to the commandments.

w046.function: Passive infinitive: not that he should never leave, but that he should never be taken away — the asking is against a thing done to him.

w047.function: Subjunctive as a petition, with “numquam” (w045) carrying the negation: never let it happen.

w050.function: The Father and the Spirit have already been named in the prayer, so the ending points back rather than introducing them again.

w059.function: Nominative standing with the two verbs: who as God livest and reignest.

w062.function: In sǽcula sæculórum here, per ómnia sǽcula sæculórum in the prayer before: the two endings differ, and both are printed as they stand.
